Hi Kelly / Colin —

Thanks again for the kickoff yesterday. Per our conversation I’ve pulled together a short runbook draft and a set of questions we need answered before we size the private GPU pool for ServeGrid’s inference traffic. I’m attaching the initial capacity model and a copy of the workload CSV you mentioned on the call.

Quick summary of what we want to validate before the architecture review:
- Target steady-state throughput (requests/sec and tokens/sec) and peak burst profile (seconds/minutes).
- P50/P95 latency targets per API path and acceptable tail-latency.
- Inter-region failover expectations and acceptable capacity loss under AZ failures.
- Network egress limits and whether your VPC has NAT gateway/egress bandwidth constraints.
- Data residency and whether telemetry traces can leave the VPC (for our metrics agent).

Proposed next steps:
1) You confirm the workload CSV columns we should use (I included what we discussed).
2) Colin can share a short diagram of the VPC topology and any bandwidth quotas.
3) We run a light model pass and present a recommended pool sizing + warmup strategy in a 30–45m readout.

Are you available Thursday 9/16 10:00–10:45 PT for the readout? If that works, we’ll circulate the pre-read and a runbook checklist.

Attachments: servegrid_workload_profile.csv, redwood_capacity_model_v1.xlsx, network_topo_vpc.drawio

Alex — thanks, this is great. Thursday 9/16 10:00 PT works for us. I attached a slightly cleaned workload export that includes "concurrency_profile" and "payload_size_bytes" per route. A couple clarifications up front:

- Target: our product team wants a 95th percentile response time <= 300ms for the core classify route, and p95 <= 800ms for large-summary jobs (these are allowed to be slower).
- Background: typical steady-state is ~180 rps across the cluster (mixed routes), with predictable customer-driven spikes up to ~850 rps for ~3–7 minutes after marketing campaigns.
- We do expect cross-region failover during maintenance windows; acceptable degradation is 40% capacity for up to 20 minutes while failover completes.
- Network: our egress is currently limited to 4 Gbps through the primary NAT. We’ve got a ticket open on our side to evaluate increasing that, but that’s what you should assume for now. Colin will share the VPC diagram.

ProcureOps flagged a few standard commercial asks: SLA language on throughput, and how dedicated capacity is scheduled. We can surface that in the readout.

From: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.ai>

Alex / team — quick technical readout in advance of Thursday. Putting the high-level recommendations here so we can iterate before the meeting.

Summary conclusions (short):
- Baseline recommended pool: 24x A100-80GB equivalent GPUs (quantized T/FP16 runtimes assumed) to meet steady-state 180 rps with p95 headroom.
- Burst headroom: reserve an additional 6 GPUs (~25% headroom) as an on-prem reserved burst pool that can be auto-enabled for up to 10 minutes per surge. Combined gives capacity for ~800–900 rps depending on request mix and median token lengths.
- Network: with a 4 Gbps egress limit we must aggressively favor NVMe/host-local batching and prefix caching to avoid saturating egress. Estimated avg egress per token = 0.06 KB with compressed payloads; with 850 rps and average 120 tokens/request we project ~6.1 Gbps if naive. With batching and in-server aggregation we can bring that under 4 Gbps.

Sizing rationale / calculations (abbreviated):
- Perf baseline: 1 A100 equiv sustains ~40–55 rps for classify routes at median token length 40; for large-summary jobs that drops to ~8–12 rps. We assume a mixed workload: 70% classify/short, 30% large-summary.
- Using weighted average and target p95 margin, 24 GPUs covers steady state; adding 6 GPUs covers the 3–7 minute spikes with headroom for cache warmup.
- Warmup plan: persistent KV cache layer with active prefix warming. Recommend a 90–120s pre-warm window for any scheduled campaign bursts; for unscheduled bursts we rely on quick ramp + fallback to smaller model variants to keep latency within 800ms.

Network and deployment notes:
- Put the metrics/agent (read-only telemetry) behind a VPC endpoint to keep traces internal where possible. If telemetry must egress, we need consent for sampled traces only.
- Autoscale behavior: scale-by-GPU-count with small incremental increments (2 GPU steps) to avoid partial-GPU fragmentation. Use request-queueing with max-queue-depth alarm to trigger model-variant fallback at 150% of baseline queue size.
- Fallbacks: 1) degrade to a quantized model variant (saves ~2.2x tokens/sec cost), 2) route non-critical large-summary jobs to a lower-priority queue with relaxed latency.

Open questions for ServeGrid before the readout:
- Can your infra team temporarily raise egress to 6–8 Gbps during campaign windows? If yes, you can reduce reserved GPUs by ~20%.
- Do you want adaptive autoscale (Redwood handles burst by default) or hard caps at committed levels? Marissa, please advise on default commercial posture.

Pre-read link: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/servegrid-capacity-preread (I pushed the quick calc tab there, file redwood_capacity_model_v1.xlsx)

-Vivek
